title: Hadley v. Baxendale
lead: A carrier’s delayed delivery of a broken shaft prolongs a mill’s shutdown. The millers can trace lost profits to the delay, but the court asks what risks the carriage contract gave the carrier reason to anticipate.

actors.name: Hadley and another proprietor
actors.role: Operators of the City Steam-Mills at Gloucester.

actors.name: Joyce & Co.
actors.role: Greenwich engineers who needed the broken shaft to make its replacement.

actors.name: Baxendale and the other defendants
actors.role: Operators of Pickford & Co., the carriers.

proceedings: The jury awarded £25 beyond the £25 the carriers paid into court.
The Court of Exchequer made the rule for a new trial absolute, requiring an instruction excluding lost profits on the circumstances it treated as communicated.
limits: This is a transformation of the canonical historical brief, not a new opinion audit. The report’s trial narrative and judgment characterize notice differently; both are preserved. Victoria Laundry supplies a later editorially reproduced interpretation, not Hadley’s own explanation. No separate opinion or numerical vote is reported.

review.basis: Individually written and compared with the canonical full brief; no new independent opinion audit claimed.

sections.title: A broken shaft stops the mill
sections.cue: Why did carrying the old shaft affect the date of reopening?
paragraphs: Hadley and another proprietor ran the City Steam-Mills in Gloucester. Their steam engine’s crankshaft broke, stopping operations on May 11; the fracture was discovered on May 12. Joyce & Co., the Greenwich engineers who had manufactured the engine, needed the broken shaft as a pattern so that a replacement would fit the surviving machinery. Until the old shaft arrived, they could not make that replacement.

On May 13 the millers sent a servant to Pickford & Co., the carriers operated by Baxendale and the other defendants. According to the report’s trial narrative, the servant told the receiving clerk that the mill had stopped and that the shaft must go immediately. The clerk said receipt before noon would secure arrival in Greenwich the following day. The millers delivered the shaft before noon the next day, paid £2 4s, and requested any special entry needed to hasten it.

Neglect delayed delivery. The replacement consequently reached Gloucester several days later than it otherwise would have, prolonging the shutdown. The millers alleged five additional days of delay, lost sales and profits, purchases of flour to supply some customers, and wages paid to idle employees. They claimed £300; those categories were allegations, not separately calculated awards.

sections.title: The jury awards additional compensation
sections.cue: What question did the carriers preserve?
paragraphs: The millers’ declaration originally had two counts. They discontinued the count alleging a promise to deliver on a specified second day. The surviving count alleged failure to use due care and diligence to deliver within a reasonable time.

The carriers paid £25 into court as satisfaction; the millers said that was insufficient. At the Gloucester Assizes, Justice Crompton left damages generally to the jury despite the carriers’ objection that lost profits were too remote. The jury awarded another £25. The carriers obtained a rule nisi asking for a new trial because of the instruction.

sections.title: The parties dispute the limits of compensation
sections.cue: Why was actual causation insufficient by itself?
paragraphs: In the Court of Exchequer, the millers argued that profits lost during stoppage were the natural, necessary consequence of delay and their only actual loss. They stressed notice to the clerk and compared cases involving late mill construction and detention of workmen’s tools. Judges Parke, Alderson, and Martin questioned counsel about foreseeability, disproportionate consequences, and the difference between making machinery operational and transporting one part.

The carriers answered that damages did not include every consequence causally following a breach. Notice to a receiving clerk, they argued, did not transform an ordinary carriage undertaking into an assumption of all nondelivery risks. A merchant supplying coal, for example, might not know that immediate delivery was needed to keep a business operating. They sought exclusion of profits and, if no other loss was proved, nominal damages.

sections.title: The court defines ordinary and communicated special risks
sections.cue: How would the new trial’s damages inquiry be limited?
paragraphs: Baron Alderson delivered the court’s judgment. A jury’s power to assess damages needed a legal boundary: otherwise the same breach could produce radically different liabilities from undisclosed circumstances. Recoverable loss must fairly and reasonably arise naturally in the usual course from breach, or have been reasonably contemplated by both parties at formation as its probable result.

Communication of special circumstances could make their ordinary consequences recoverable. Without that knowledge, the breaching party ordinarily contemplated only losses common to the multitude of transactions. Notice gave parties an opportunity to arrange special terms for increased risk. Established rules for nonpayment of money or failure to convey good title fit the principle because contracting parties could be presumed to contemplate those known rules.

Applying that approach, the court characterized what the carriers knew as shipment of a broken shaft by the millers who owned it. That alone did not disclose that the entire mill’s earnings depended on prompt carriage. A mill might have a spare shaft in use or being installed, or other defective machinery might prevent operation anyway. These were possibilities explaining ordinary expectations, not findings about this mill.

The court accepted that the old shaft was needed as a model, its replacement was the sole cause of stoppage, and delay caused lost profits. But it treated those special dependencies as neither communicated nor known at formation. Causation therefore did not establish that profits were within recoverable contractual risk.

sections.title: The notice tension remains, and a new trial is ordered
sections.cue: What precisely did the court decide?
paragraphs: That application sits uneasily beside the earlier report that the clerk was told the mill had stopped and delivery was urgent. The judgment did not expressly reconcile the accounts. Its holding rests on the communicated circumstances as the court characterized them; it does not establish that notice of an urgent shutdown could never disclose a special risk. A later decision, Victoria Laundry, interpreted Hadley as rejecting the relevant notice evidence, but that later interpretation is not an explanation supplied in Hadley itself.

The Court of Exchequer made the rule absolute and ordered a new trial. The jury had to be instructed to exclude these lost profits. The court did not calculate a substitute award, enter final judgment for zero damages, or adopt the carriers’ nominal-damages request as its complete decree.

sources.pinpoint: 9 Ex. 344, 355–356; assigned editorial discussion at printed 1019
